podcast.body: Co-written years earlier with Ian Gomm, this song had been recorded in rougher forms before its 1979 release. It is described as a "perfect pop song" that is tight, catchy, and under three minutes. "Cruel to Be Kind" exemplified the emerging New Wave sound, which pushed back against the late 1970s rock trend of long songs, big solos, and a perceived need for everything to be "super important." New Wave, and this song in particular, prioritized efficiency: a quick intro, verse, chorus, verse, and then out, with no wasted space. This approach made it accessible for radio listeners and casual fans, offering something new that wasn't overly complex. It made it to number 12 on the Billboard Top 40 in 1979. "Cruel to be kind doesn't seem like it's anything revolutionary, it's very tight, it's catchy, it's under three minutes, that's kind of the point because by the time we get to the late 1970s, rock had gotten very big, we had long songs, big solos, we got this idea that everything had to be super important."

Rupert Holmes considered using this title for one of his songs but refrained because Nick Lowe already had a song with that title. "Then he tried something with cruel to be kind, but no Nick Lowe has a song with that title."

podcast.body: This song was a hit single for Nick Lowe in the summer of 1979, appearing on his gold-certified album "Labor of Lust" in Canada. It exemplifies Lowe's Powerpop style, which has been highly influential, earning him recognition from contemporary artists like Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys. "Nick Lowe with Cruell to Be Kind from the summer of 1979."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was co-written by Lowe and his Brinsley Schwarz bandmate Ian Gomm during their time together. Lowe modeled it after "The Love I Lost," an early disco hit by Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes, which he admired and sought to adapt into a power pop song. The Brinsley's version was never released, but Lowe later re-recorded it with his Rockpile bandmate Dave Edmonds. What might have been an "odd fit for the pub rock era" proved "ideal for the New Wave era." Released in the summer of 1979, "Cruel to Be Kind" reached number 12 in both the US and the UK. It remains Lowe's only top 40 hit in America, making him, by definition, a one-hit wonder there. Lowe has stated that he still loves the song and continues to play it live. "Crull to be kind."

podcast.body: This song was the hit that made Nick Lowe a "one-hit wonder." Despite its success, Lowe had not scored a gold or platinum album of his own until the unexpected financial windfall from "The Bodyguard" soundtrack. "The man whose cruel to be kind had made him a one-hit wonder."
